back: Scalar: magnitude only, combined by ordinary algebra (distance, mass, temperature). Vector: magnitude + direction, obeys the triangle/parallelogram law (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force).
When they have the same magnitude AND the same direction. Vectors can be shifted parallel to themselves freely — they have no fixed location.

front: Multiplication of a vector by a real number λ
back: λ > 0: magnitude ×λ, same direction. λ < 0: magnitude ×|λ|, opposite direction. λA is a vector; its dimension is the product of the dimension of λ and A.
Commutative A + B = B + A; associative A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C; null vector A + (−A) = 0; subtraction A − B = A + (−B).

front: Ruler's combo: wind + rain umbrella problem
back: Resultant velocity has the magnitude sqrt(35² + 12²) = 37 m s⁻¹, at angle tan⁻¹(12/35) ≈ 19° with the vertical — the boy holds the umbrella tilted toward the east.
A = Aₓî + A_yĵ with Aₓ = A cosθ, A_y = A sinθ; recovery A = sqrt(Aₓ² + A_y²), tanθ = A_y/Aₓ. In 3-D add A_z k̂ with A = sqrt(Aₓ² + A_y² + A_z²).
Magnitude 1, directions of the x-, y-, z-axes, mutually perpendicular, dimensionless and unitless. Any vector A = |A| n̂ where n̂ is a unit vector.
Add component-wise: R = A + B → Rₓ = Aₓ + Bₓ, R_y = A_y + B_y. For T = a + b − c, subtract with the appropriate signs. Compare with the graphical (triangle/parallelogram) method.
R² = A² + B² + 2AB cosθ (law of cosines); law of sines R/sinθ = A/sinβ = B/sinα; tanα = B sinθ/(A + B cosθ).
v = lim(Δt→0) Δr/Δt = dr/dt. Always tangential to the path, in the direction of motion. Components vₓ = dx/dt, v_y = dy/dt; v = sqrt(vₓ² + v_y²).
a = lim(Δt→0) Δv/Δt = dv/dt with aₓ = dvₓ/dt, a_y = dv_y/dt. Unlike 1-D, v and a need not be collinear — the angle between them may be anything from 0° to 180°.
v = 3î + 4tĵ; a = 4ĵ (constant). At t = 1 s, v = 3î + 4ĵ → |v| = 5 m s⁻¹ at tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53° to the x-axis.
v = v₀ + at; r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at². The motion separates into independent 1-D problems along each axis (components decouple).
Horizontal: x = (v₀cosθ₀)t, vₓ constant. Vertical: y = (v₀sinθ₀)t − ½gt², v_y = v₀sinθ₀ − gt. Galileo: horizontal motion and vertical free fall are simultaneous and independent.
y = x tanθ₀ − gx²/(2v₀²cos²θ₀) — of the form y = ax + bx², hence THE PATH OF A PROJECTILE IS A PARABOLA.
t_m = v₀sinθ₀/g; T_f = 2t_m; h_m = (v₀sinθ₀)²/2g; R = v₀² sin(2θ₀)/g. R is a maximum at θ₀ = 45°, R_m = v₀²/g.
R = v₀² sin(2θ₀)/g; for θ₀ = 45° ± α, sin(2θ₀) = sin(90° ± 2α) = cos 2α in both cases — Galileo's Two New Sciences observation.

front: Stone thrown horizontally from 490 m cliff
back: Vertical drop decides the time: t = sqrt(2h/g) = 10 s regardless of vₓ = 15 m s⁻¹. Impact components: (15, −98) m s⁻¹ → speed ≈ 99 m s⁻¹.

front: Uniform circular motion: what is constant?
back: Speed v constant and angular speed ω constant; only the DIRECTION of velocity changes, so there is a centripetal acceleration towards the centre.
a_c = v²/R = ω²R = 4π²ν²R, directed towards the centre. ω = 2π/T = 2πν; v = Rω = 2πR/T.

front: Kinematic equations in uniform circular motion
back: DO NOT apply — the centripetal acceleration is not a constant vector (its direction keeps turning towards the centre), and constant-acceleration equations require constant a.
Net acceleration is radial only for UNIFORM circular motion; velocity is always tangential; the acceleration averaged over a full cycle is the null vector.

Displacement is the straight-line vector between initial and final points — the same for every path between the points (e.g. 400 m across the circular park); path length is 400 m only for the direct route.
